The aim of the present paper is to provide a global presentation of the theory of special Finsler manifolds. We introduce and investigate globally (or intrinsically, free from local coordinates) many of the most important and most commonly used special Finsler manifolds: locally Minkowskian, Berwald, Landesberg, general Landesberg, $P$-reducible, $C$-reducible, semi-$C$-reducible, quasi-$C$-reducible, $P^{*}$-Finsler, $C^{h}$-recurrent, $C^{v}$-recurrent, $C^{0}$-recurrent, $S^{v}$-recurrent, $S^{v}$-recurrent of the second order, $C_{2}$-like, $S_{3}$-like, $S_{4}$-like, $P_{2}$-like, $R_{3}$-like, $P$-symmetric, $h$-isotropic, of scalar curvature, of constant curvature, of $p$-scalar curvature, of $s$-$ps$-curvature. The global definitions of these special Finsler manifolds are introduced. Various relationships between the different types of the considered special Finsler manifolds are found. Many local results, known in the literature, are proved globally and several new results are obtained. As a by-product, interesting identities and properties concerning the torsion tensor fields and the curvature tensor fields are deduced. Although our investigation is entirely global, we provide; for comparison reasons, an appendix presenting a local counterpart of our global approach and the local definitions of the special Finsler spaces considered.

It presents and studies, in an intrinsic manner independent of local coordinates, many of the most significant and frequently used classes of special Finsler manifolds, including locally Minkowskian, Berwald, Landesberg, general Landesberg, \(P\)-reducible, \(C\)-reducible, semi-\(C\)-reducible, quasi-\(C\)-reducible, \(P^{*}\)-Finsler, \(C^{h}\)-recurrent, \(C^{v}\)-recurrent, \(C^{0}\)-recurrent, \(S^{v}\)-recurrent, second-order \(S^{v}\)-recurrent, \(C_{2}\)-like, \(S_{3}\)-like, \(S_{4}\)-like, \(P_{2}\)-like, \(R_{3}\)-like, \(P\)-symmetric, \(h\)-isotropic manifolds, as well as manifolds of scalar curvature, constant curvature, \(p\)-scalar curvature, and \(s\)-\(ps\)-curvature.

The work formulates global definitions for all of these categories of special Finsler manifolds and establishes a range of connections among them. Within this framework, the paper introduces and investigates global definitions for many significant classes of special Finsler manifolds. These include various types that are traditionally defined and studied through local expressions, but are here reformulated in a way that is independent of the choice of coordinates. This global perspective makes it possible to analyze their geometric meaning more transparently.

A central part of the paper is devoted to establishing relationships among the different classes of special Finsler manifolds under consideration. By comparing their defining properties and examining the implications between them, the paper clarifies how these classes are connected and how certain conditions may lead from one type of special Finsler structure to another.

The work also revisits many known local results and proves them within the global framework. In doing so, it not only confirms the consistency of the coordinate-free approach with the classical local theory, but also extends the scope of several results. Moreover, the paper obtains a number of new results that follow naturally from the global formulation.

In addition, the paper derives several identities and properties related to torsion and curvature tensors, which play a fundamental role in the geometry of Finsler manifolds. These tensorial results contribute to a deeper understanding of the structures being studied. Finally, the paper includes an appendix that compares the global approach with traditional local definitions, helping to bridge the two perspectives and demonstrating the equivalence or correspondence between them where appropriate.

**The Finsler-Minkowskian Perspective**

The Finsler-Minkowskian framework is an important idea in modern geometry, extending classical concepts from Euclidean and Riemannian spaces. In ordinary Euclidean geometry, distances are measured using a fixed quadratic formula. Minkowskian geometry generalizes this by allowing a broader notion of length, while Finsler geometry takes the idea even further by permitting the measurement of distance to vary from point to point and direction to direction.

In a Minkowskian space, the length of a vector is defined by a norm that does not necessarily come from an inner product. This means that the “unit sphere” may not be a perfect circle or sphere in the Euclidean sense; instead, it can have a more general convex shape. The Finsler approach builds on this by assigning such norms smoothly across a manifold, creating a flexible geometric structure.

The significance of the Finsler-Minkowskian viewpoint lies in its ability to describe spaces where movement, distance, or physical behavior depends on direction. This makes it useful not only in pure mathematics but also in areas such as physics, optimization, and theoretical models of anisotropic media. By moving beyond the limitations of standard metric geometry, the Finsler-Minkowskian setting provides a richer language for understanding complex spaces and the paths within them.
